<div class="banner">
<strong>Bottom line:</strong> Two weeks at 31 °C weakened *Acropora pulchra* fragments and mostly blocked the last regrowth step: budding new corallites, the small skeletal cups that form on a rebuilt tip. Wounds still sealed. Source patch C was much less heat sensitive than source patches A and D.<br>
<strong>Genetic caveat:</strong> Rachael's preliminary RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) DNA-marker file shows C grouping together, but A and D are mixed. For now, A, C, and D are source patches, not confirmed genetic individuals.
</div>

We heated *Acropora pulchra* fragments at <span class="t28">28 °C</span> or <span class="t31">31 °C</span>. We clipped the growing tip on half of them. For two weeks, we tracked healing, growth, coral condition, and algal symbionts, the algae living in coral tissue. Tank temperature has to hold before the biological comparisons mean anything. Whole-fragment condition shows whether heat weakened the coral. Regrowth timing shows which repair step failed. Source-patch and DNA-marker results ask whether heat tolerance is tied to coral identity.

Rachael's preliminary DNA-marker check changes the genetic wording. The markers come from RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data. They are single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), which are single DNA-letter differences. Source patch C looks genetically consistent in that file, but source patches A and D look mixed. For now, this summary treats A, C, and D as source patches, not confirmed genetic individuals.

Every number here comes from `output/tables/20_master_results.csv`; the full write-up with limitations is in `RESULTS.docx`. Coral photos and the design figure are from the project deck (M. Brzezinski); see `img/SLIDE_IMAGES_INDEX.docx`.

## The experiment

- 8 tanks: four held at <span class="t28">28 °C</span>, four at <span class="t31">31 °C</span>
- Half the fragments had the growing tip clipped; half were left unwounded
- 3 field source patches: A, C, D. A source patch is where the parent material came from; these patches are not yet confirmed genetic individuals.
- Tracked at Days 1, 3, 10, 15

```{r, fig.cap=cap_design}
knitr::include_graphics(img("slide05_experimental_design.png"))
```

We wounded each clipped fragment by removing the growing tip. The Day 0 photo below shows the fresh cut surface.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_wound_day0}
knitr::include_graphics(img("slide14_morphology_heated_D0.png"))
```

## What we found

### 1. The +3 °C temperature difference held

Tanks stayed close to <span class="t28">28 °C</span> vs <span class="t31">31 °C</span> for the whole run. The tanks maintained the intended +3 °C difference.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_apex}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("08_apex_temperature.png"))
```

Tank temperatures did not drift enough to explain the later coral differences.

### 2. Heat, not wounding, drove the whole-coral decline

Under <span class="t31">31 °C</span>, corals had lower photosynthesis-efficiency scores, called Fv/Fm, paled, gained less skeletal mass, and lost algal symbionts.

Clipped fragments did not lose much more condition than unwounded fragments. Photosynthesis score, color, growth, and symbiont density changed mainly with temperature. The whole-fragment decline is therefore mainly a heat effect, not a general effect of clipping the tip.

- Photosynthesis score and color declined through time under heat.
- Symbiont density dropped sharply over the two weeks.
- Skeletal mass gain was **34% lower** at <span class="t31">31 °C</span>. The tank-level test compares tanks rather than individual fragments. The tank-level *p*-value was 0.057, so the growth result is suggestive rather than firm.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_growth}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("05_buoyant_weight_growth.png"))
```

```{r, fig.cap=cap_symbiont}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("06_symbiont_density_by_day.png"))
```

Clipping the tip did not make the whole coral collapse. Heat caused most of the decline across the whole fragment.

### 3. Heat did not stop wound sealing, but it blocked new corallites

Wounds seal at the same rate whether or not corals are heated. Heated corals also usually rebuild the main polyp and a tip. What they often fail to do is bud new corallites, the small new skeletal cups that show true regrowth.

The Day 15 breakdown for wounded corals shows where heat changed regrowth. Values are the percent of fragments that reached each step; sample size = 12 fragments per temperature.

| Day 15 sign in wounded fragments | 28 °C | 31 °C |
|---|---|---|
| Wound sealed | 100% | 100% |
| Main polyp rebuilt | 100% | 100% |
| Tip present | 92% | 92% |
| Tip grew outward | 92% | 75% |
| **New corallites budded on the tip** | **100%** | **33%** |

The smaller microscope-photo data set gives the same result. By Day 15, new corallites appeared in 100% of 28 °C fragments but only 25% of 31 °C fragments, matching the main photo data set (100% vs 33%).

The early healing steps, and even tip rebuilding, are nearly identical between temperatures. The difference is the final step: budding *new* corallites on the tip. That is what "not regenerated" means here. The timing analyses test how quickly fragments reached that step.

- New-corallite budding stalls under heat. One timing analysis says budding took **1.32× longer** under heat (*p* = 1.4e-7). A second timing analysis gives a hazard ratio (HR) of **0.22**. HR is a rate comparison. Values below 1 mean heated fragments reached this step more slowly.
- **67%** of heated corals closed the wound and reformed a tip but never budded new corallites, vs **0%** at 28 °C

```{r, fig.cap=cap_morph_km}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("14_morphology_KM.png"))
```

A closed wound is not the same thing as a regenerated tip. If we scored only wound sealing, we would miss the main heat effect.

In the photo timeline below, both temperatures seal the wound and rebuild a tip. The difference is whether *new corallites* bud on that tip. Look for those small new cups, not just the tip itself.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_timeline}
knitr::include_graphics(img("slide15_morphology_timeline.jpg"))
```

The looping time-lapse shows the same sequence from Day 0 to Day 15. The 28 °C fragment on the left heals and buds new corallites. The 31 °C fragment on the right heals and rebuilds a tip but stalls before new-corallite budding.

### 4. Source patch C was hurt less by heat

The three source patches did not respond alike. Fragments from source patch **C** kept their photosynthesis score, color, and symbionts far better than fragments from source patches A and D.

Source patch C did not merely start healthier. Heat hurt C less. Photosynthesis score, color, and symbiont density all show that source patch C had a smaller heat penalty. Growth changed in the same direction, but the growth result is weaker.

- Heat hit source patch C about **2.7–3.5× less** than source patches A and D, depending on the measurement. For example, symbiont loss was about 3.5× steeper in A and D, and photosynthesis-score loss was about 2.6× steeper in A and D.
- When the four whole-coral condition measurements are summarized together, source patch C changed much less under heat: C = 1.02 vs A = 3.71 and D = 3.38. Bigger values mean a larger change from 28 °C.

The summary plot below gives the clearest view. A heat penalty means how much worse 31 °C was than 28 °C. The plot averages those penalties by source patch and measurement type.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_source_summary}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19e_source_heat_penalty_summary.png"))
```

In the summary plot, source patch C stays near zero overall. Source patches A and D have bigger condition, growth, and regrowth penalties. Wound-sealing traits sit near or below zero because heat did not slow sealing itself.

Source patch C's advantage is heat tolerance, not simply better condition in every treatment. The question is how much each source patch changes when heated.

For the whole-coral condition measurements alone, source patch C has the smaller heat penalty in every measurement.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_source_physiology}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19f_source_physiology_heat_penalties.png"))
```

The next plot shows the individual condition and healing measurements behind the average.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_genet_dashboard}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19_genet_dashboard.png"))
```

The last plot in this section shows healing and regrowth only.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_wound_heat}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("19d_wound_healing_heat_penalties.png"))
```

**How the heat-penalty score is built** (`code/19`)

The score has two steps.

**Step 1: calculate the heat effect for each source patch within each measurement.**

For whole-coral condition and growth:

\[
\text{heat effect}_{source,measurement} =
\text{estimated value at }28^\circ\text{C} - \text{estimated value at }31^\circ\text{C}
\]

For these measurements, higher values mean better coral condition or growth. A positive heat effect means the source patch did worse at 31 °C.

For wound sealing and regrowth timing, the timing analysis first gives a hazard ratio (HR). HR is the rate at which a healing or regrowth step appeared at 31 °C compared with 28 °C.

\[
\text{heat effect}_{source,measurement} =
-\log(\text{HR}_{31^\circ\text{C} / 28^\circ\text{C}})
\]

If HR is below 1, the step happened more slowly at 31 °C, and the heat effect becomes positive.

**Step 2: put each measurement on the same scale, then average.**

\[
\text{scaled heat penalty}_{source,measurement} =
\frac{\text{heat effect}_{source,measurement}}
{\max(|\text{heat effect}_{A,measurement}|,\ |\text{heat effect}_{C,measurement}|,\ |\text{heat effect}_{D,measurement}|)}
\]

This makes the largest source-patch difference within each measurement equal to 1 in size. It keeps the sign: positive means worse or slower at 31 °C; negative means better or faster at 31 °C.

\[
\text{source heat-penalty score}_{source} =
\text{mean of scaled heat penalties across usable measurements}
\]

The score therefore does not average raw values collected on different days. It first asks, within each measurement, how much worse 31 °C was than 28 °C for each source patch. Then it puts that measurement on the same 0-to-1 scale as the others. This score ranks the three source patches. It is not a formal statistical test. Heat-penalty values averaged: A = 9, C = 10, D = 10. Heat-penalty score: C = 0.01 vs A = 0.56 and D = 0.43.

**Trade-off checks**

The trade-off checks are exploratory. The one possible cost is growth: source patch C grew less at 28 °C, but lost less growth under heat. We do not see the same cost for regeneration. Heated wounded fragments that budded new corallites did not grow less. Source patch C also had the lowest whole-fragment heat penalty and the most new-corallite budding under heat.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_tradeoff_summary}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("35_tradeoff_summary.png"))
```

### 5. What Rachael's preliminary DNA-marker file changes

Rachael's 2 Sept 2026 preliminary file uses DNA markers from RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). The markers are single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), or single DNA-letter differences. In that file, the source-patch labels are not all single genetic individuals. Source patch C falls into its own DNA-marker cluster, but source patches A and D are mixed. Source patches A and D appear to include several possible genetic individuals, and some DNA-marker clusters are shared between them.

The result does not disappear, but we should name the groups more carefully. We should say **source patch C was less heat sensitive**, not **genet C was less heat sensitive**. A genet is one confirmed cloned genetic individual, and we do not have that final call yet. Once the final genetic file is ready, we can join it to the coral-measurement table. That will let us ask whether source patch C still looks heat tolerant when genetically similar fragments are compared more directly.

Rachael's file (`PRELIM_LTH_genoclusters.csv`) lets us start that check, but it is still **preliminary**. The file matched all 144 RNA-seq libraries by fragment ID, the number assigned to each coral fragment. A library is a tissue sample prepared for sequencing. The file shows:

- Source patch C: **48/48** libraries in preliminary SNP cluster 1.
- Source patch A: 48 libraries split across clusters 4, 5, 6, and 7; cluster 4 dominates.
- Source patch D: 48 libraries split across clusters 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8.
- Clusters 4 and 5 are shared between A and D.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_prelim_snp_structure}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("32_prelim_snp_structure.png"))
```

Source patch C is straightforward in the preliminary DNA-marker file; source patches A and D are not. That is why this summary says "source patch C" instead of "genet C."

The preliminary DNA-marker clusters help label possible genetic groups, but they are not new treatment groups. The experiment was balanced by source patch. The clusters were found afterward, and they split A and D unevenly.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_prelim_snp_design}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("32_prelim_snp_design_balance.png"))
```

The preliminary DNA-marker clusters tell us what to check next. They should not be treated like treatments we assigned evenly at the start.

The main limit is whether the same coral fragment has both data types. These 144 RNA-seq/SNP fragments directly match the symbiont-density tissue samples. They do **not** directly match the fragments measured for photosynthesis score, color, growth, whole-tip healing photos, or microscope photos. That leaves symbiont density as the only direct preliminary SNP-by-measurement check. For the other measurements, we can compare source patch C with source patches A and D within each treatment. We cannot yet compare DNA markers and those measurements fragment by fragment unless those fragments are sequenced too.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_prelim_snp_symbiont}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("32_prelim_snp_symbiont_heat_effects.png"))
```

At this stage, symbiont density is the only direct fragment-by-fragment DNA-marker check. It agrees with the source-patch result: source patch C/cluster 1 loses fewer symbionts under heat.

### 6. The heat treatment was long-term, but below the acute heat limit

<span class="t31">31 °C</span> sits about **4.4 °C below** the acute heat limit for this species at this site. That heat limit is the half-drop temperature (ED50) for Fv/Fm, the photosynthesis-efficiency score. ED50 is the temperature where that score drops halfway. The mean in Cunning et al. 2024 was 35.4 °C. This was weeks of heat stress below the acute bleaching threshold, not a short heat shock.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_thermal_context}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("26_thermal_context.png"))
```

31 °C was not an extreme acute shock. Moderate, sustained heat was enough to disrupt regeneration.

## Take-homes

- Heat drove the whole-fragment response. At 31 °C, fragments had lower photosynthesis score, paler color, fewer symbionts, and lower skeletal growth. Wounding added little to those whole-fragment changes.
- Heat did not stop wound sealing. It mostly blocked the final regrowth step: new corallites budded on 33% of heated wounded fragments by Day 15, compared with 100% at 28 °C. The smaller microscope-photo data set showed the same failure, 25% at 31 °C versus 100% at 28 °C.
- Source patch C had the smallest heat penalty. Source patches A and D lost more condition, growth, and regrowth under heat.
- The trade-off checks show one possible cost but no regeneration cost so far. Source patch C may trade faster growth at 28 °C for steadier growth under heat, but it did not regenerate worse.
- Rachael's preliminary DNA-marker file changes the wording, not the main result. Source patch C is genetically coherent in the preliminary file, while source patches A and D split across several clusters. Treat A, C, and D as source-patch labels for now, not confirmed genetic individuals.
- Symbiont density is the only direct fragment-by-fragment DNA-marker measurement we can test now. It agrees with the source-patch results: source patch C/cluster 1 loses fewer symbionts under heat.
- The <span class="t31">31 °C</span> treatment was long-term heat stress about 4.4 °C below the acute heat threshold, not a short heat shock.
